unit.subject: English
unit.unitOverview: Unit 6 is about the people who keep a community working: the helpers, the leaders, and the newcomers. You will meet a caretaker, a carpenter, an engineer and a merchant, then governors, senators, lawyers and the military, and finally artists, photographers, messengers, refugees, immigrants, tenants and consumers. You will use the Present Simple to say what each person does, should and mustn't to give advice and rules, prepositions to say where people go, and the past tenses to retell what happened. By the end you will describe the helpers in your own town, just as Amal does in the story “The Community Parade”.
unit.learningPath:
Start with the Vocabulary section and learn one of the four word groups each day.
Work through the six Grammar lessons in order, saying every example aloud.
Read the two Reading passages, listen to the Interview, then read the Story “The Community Parade”.
Answer the Comprehension questions, then move through Speaking, Writing and Activities.
Play the Games and take the Quiz, then finish with My Progress and the Self-Assessment.

readings.title: The People of Our Town
readings.setting: A familiar town: school, market, river and town hall
readings.passageScript: Every town is full of people who play important roles. Early in the morning, the caretaker cleans the school before the pupils arrive. His name is Idris, and for eleven years he has swept the same corridors and unlocked the same gate before the first bell rings. In the market, a merchant sells fresh fruit while a carpenter mends a wooden stall. Their names are Omar and Karim, and their stalls stand side by side, filling the square with the smell of oranges and the tap of a hammer. Near the river, an engineer checks the new bridge, and a labourer carries heavy stones. Elena the engineer studies every bolt with a careful eye, while her helper stacks the stones exactly where she points. At the town hall, the governor reads a new plan. She is deciding how the town's money should be spent this year, on new roads or on a bigger library. Close by, a lawyer helps a family understand the law. He reads the difficult words slowly, until even the youngest child in the room understands. We do not always notice these people, but our town could not work without them. Every one of them helps us to live, to learn, and to stay safe, from the first light of morning until the streetlamps glow at night.
readings.reviewStatus: Needs re-review (content updated for self-sufficiency pass)

readings.title: Two Neighbours: A Refugee and an Immigrant
readings.setting: Two neighbouring homes on the same street
readings.passageScript: Theo and his family are refugees. They left their home because it was not safe. They travelled a long way to find a peaceful place, crossing three borders and sleeping in strange rooms before they finally reached our town. Now Theo lives at the end of our street, in a small house with a garden full of tomato plants that he waters every evening after school. Next door lives Omar, who came here as an immigrant. He moved to our town to open a market stall and build a better life. He wanted his children to grow up somewhere calm and safe, with good schools and kind neighbours. Every morning before the sun is fully up, Omar arranges baskets of mangoes and bags of spices, and he always saves the sweetest fruit for the children on his street. Theo's mother explains the difference simply. “A refugee runs from danger. An immigrant walks towards a dream. We should welcome both, because everyone deserves a safe home and a kind neighbour.” Theo says he is learning to feel at home here, one football match and one new word at a time, and Omar says our market would not be the same without him.
readings.reviewStatus: Needs re-review (content updated for self-sufficiency pass)

readings.title: An Interview with a Community Helper
readings.setting: A riverside building site and the school newspaper desk
readings.passageScript:
Nora: “Good morning, Elena! Thank you for talking to our school newspaper today.”
Elena: “Good morning, Nora! I am happy to help.”
Nora: “What does an engineer do?”
Elena: “An engineer designs and builds things like roads, bridges, and machines. I am building a new bridge for our town.”
Nora: “That sounds like a big job. How long will it take?”
Elena: “About six more months, if the weather stays kind to us.”
Nora: “Where do you work?”
Elena: “I work near the river, and sometimes in an office. Today I am standing by the water, checking the plans.”
Nora: “What do you wear to stay safe on the site?”
Elena: “A bright helmet and strong boots, every single day, without exception.”
Nora: “Why is your work important?”
Elena: “Because a strong bridge helps people cross the river safely. You mustn't build in a hurry. You should plan carefully and check everything twice.”
Nora: “Thank you, Elena. I can't wait to walk across your bridge when it opens!”
Elena: “Neither can I, Nora. Save me a seat at the opening!”
readings.reviewStatus: Needs re-review (content updated for self-sufficiency pass)

readings.title: The Community Parade
readings.setting: A town centre on the morning of the Unity Parade
readings.passageScript:
It was the morning of our town's Unity Parade. Amal stood beside her mother, watching people gather across the wide street. Everyone was getting ready for the big day. Amal's school had been chosen to make posters about the important jobs in their community.
Amal held up a sign. “This one says, ‘Engineer — builds bridges and machines.’”
Her friend Nora smiled. “Mine says, ‘Caretaker — keeps our school clean.’”
Amal looked at her older brother. “Adam, where is your sign?”
He laughed. “I made two! One for the military, because they protect us, and one for the refugees who moved here last year.”
“That is kind,” said Teacher Yasmin. “We must show respect to all people, especially those who help us and those who need our help.”
The class walked towards the centre of town. They passed the bakery, the market, and the community hall, where families waved and took photos. Everyone stood by the road, ready to watch.
The parade began with the mayor, followed by the local governor. People clapped. “He works so hard,” said an old man.
Next came the military, marching proudly. A small boy asked, “Who are they?”
“They protect our country,” his mother said. “You mustn't forget their service.”
Then a woman held up a photo. “This is my son. He is a lawyer now!”
Amal whispered to Nora, “What does a lawyer do?”
“He helps people solve their problems,” Nora answered.
Suddenly, loud music played. A group of dancers went past. Among them was an artist, painting live on a big canvas.
“Wow!” said Nora. “That looks like magic.”
“It is hard work,” said Teacher Yasmin. “The artist must plan carefully and work with great care.”
“Look!” Amal pointed. “Here comes the photographer. She is taking pictures of everything.”
The woman smiled. “Say cheese!” They posed and giggled.
Then a group of immigrants came marching. They carried flags and smiled. A young man held a sign: “I travelled a long way, and I found a home here.”
Amal clapped. “Mama, what is the difference between an immigrant and a refugee?”
Her mother explained, “A refugee leaves home to stay safe. An immigrant moves to build a new life. We should welcome both.”
In the next part of the parade, someone shouted, “Here come the helpers!”
Karim the carpenter walked with his tools. Omar the merchant pushed a cart full of fruit. A labourer waved, his shirt dusty from the morning's work. And a caretaker walked proudly in his clean uniform.
Amal's sign said, “Every helper is a hero.”
A boy behind her asked, “But isn't a hero someone who saves people?”
“Yes,” said Amal. “But heroes are not only in stories. Some clean our schools, fix our roads, or bring us news.”
Just then, a bicycle bell rang. It was a messenger, holding a stack of newspapers.
“Read today's top article!” he shouted. “Local senator visits school and praises the pupils!”
Teacher Yasmin took a paper and read the first line aloud: “Young citizens learn about jobs and respect.”
Back at school, the class talked about everything they had seen.
“What did you learn?” Teacher Yasmin asked.
“I learned what a tenant is,” said Adam. “A person who rents a home.”
“And a consumer,” said Amal. “That is someone who buys things, like me at the shop!”
Teacher Yasmin smiled. “Good. And remember: everyone has a role. You should thank the people around you. You mustn't ignore them.”
Later that day, Amal wrote in her journal. She kept it in a personal place where no one else could read it:
“Today I saw artists, caretakers, and even the military. Some wore fine clothes. Others wore work shoes. But all of them help us to live, to grow, and to stay safe. We walk past them every day, but today, we noticed them.”
She paused, then added one more line:
“Next time I see the caretaker, I will say thank you. Because heroes don't always wear capes. Sometimes, they carry brooms.”

comprehension.question: Which two workers does the text place in the market, and what does each one do?
comprehension.correctAnswer: The merchant sells fresh fruit and the carpenter mends a wooden stall.
comprehension.explanation: Both workers appear in the market sentence, so the answer names them in the order the text gives.

comprehension.question: In “The People of Our Town”, which preposition tells you where the engineer checks the new bridge?
comprehension.correctAnswer: The word near, because the text says the engineer works near the river.
comprehension.explanation: Near is a place preposition, so it fixes the engineer beside the river rather than moving him along it.

comprehension.question: The text says our town could not work without them. What does that tell you about these workers?
comprehension.correctAnswer: It shows the town depends on their daily work to stay clean, safe and fair.
comprehension.explanation: The final sentence lists living, learning and staying safe, so the workers hold up ordinary town life.

comprehension.question: Why did Theo's family leave their home?
comprehension.correctAnswer: They left because their home was not safe.
comprehension.explanation: The second sentence gives the reason directly, so the answer copies the cause the text supplies.

comprehension.question: What did Omar come to our town to do?
comprehension.correctAnswer: He came to open a market stall and build a better life.
comprehension.explanation: Omar is named as the immigrant, and his two reasons sit side by side in one sentence.

comprehension.question: How does Theo's mother describe the difference between a refugee and an immigrant?
comprehension.correctAnswer: She says a refugee runs from danger while an immigrant walks towards a dream.
comprehension.explanation: Her two short sentences use running and walking to contrast escaping danger with choosing a new life.

comprehension.question: What does Elena say an engineer designs and builds?
comprehension.correctAnswer: She says an engineer designs and builds roads, bridges, and machines.
comprehension.explanation: Elena answers the reporter's first question with a list of three things, and the answer keeps all three.

comprehension.question: Where is Elena standing today, and what is she checking?
comprehension.correctAnswer: She is standing by the water and checking the plans for the bridge.
comprehension.explanation: Her second reply names the place with by and then the task, so both details come from one sentence.

comprehension.question: What advice does Elena give using should and mustn't?
comprehension.correctAnswer: She says you mustn't build in a hurry and you should plan carefully and check twice.
comprehension.explanation: The rule and the advice sit in her last reply, one telling us what is banned and one what is wise.

comprehension.question: Why had Amal's school been chosen for the parade?
comprehension.correctAnswer: The school was chosen to make posters about the important jobs in their community.
comprehension.explanation: The opening paragraph gives the school its task, which is why the class carries signs all morning.

comprehension.question: What two signs did Adam make, and what reason did he give for each?
comprehension.correctAnswer: He made one for the military because they protect us, and one for the refugees who moved here.
comprehension.explanation: Adam explains both signs in the same speech, giving protection as one reason and welcome as the other.

comprehension.question: What does Amal mean when she writes that heroes do not always wear capes?
comprehension.correctAnswer: She means ordinary helpers, such as the caretaker with his brooms, are heroes too.
comprehension.explanation: Her last journal line swaps the storybook cape for a broom, so quiet daily work counts as bravery.

grammar.title: Present Simple: describing everyday jobs
grammar.explanation: We use the Present Simple for routines, facts, and things that happen again and again. It suits jobs perfectly, because most jobs repeat every day: “The caretaker cleans the school every morning.”
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
I / you / we / they + base verb: “They build roads.”
he / she / it + verb + s: “The engineer designs bridges.”
Add es after -sh, -ch, -x or -o: “watches”, “fixes”, “goes”.
A consonant plus y becomes ies: “carry” → “carries”.
Negatives use don't / doesn't: “She doesn't work on Fridays.”
Questions use Do / Does: “Does a lawyer help people?”
grammar.commonMistake: Many writers slip into “She play football.” Keep the s for he, she and it: “She plays football.” After does the verb returns to its base form, so we ask “Does she play football?” and never “Does she plays football?”
grammar.memoryTip: Say it like a chant: “He, she, it — add an s to it!” Picture the s as a small cape that only he, she and it are allowed to wear.
grammar.practice: Write the correct Present Simple form of the verb in brackets. | The cat (sleep) ______ on the sofa every afternoon. | My mother (cook) ______ dinner in the evening. | They (play) ______ football every weekend. | The teacher (give) ______ homework on Fridays. | She (not like) ______ broccoli. | Answer key: 1. sleeps, 2. cooks, 3. play, 4. gives, 5. does not like (doesn't like).

grammar.title: Imperatives: giving clear instructions
grammar.explanation: Imperatives give a command, an instruction, or a piece of advice. They tell someone what to do, or what not to do. We use them for rules, recipes, directions, and kind advice, like “Be kind to new immigrants.”
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
Start with the verb; you do not need the word “you”: “Listen carefully.”
For a negative command, put don't before the verb: “Don't forget your lunch.”
Add please to sound polite: “Please close the door.”
Use let's when you suggest doing something together: “Let's help the new pupil.”
grammar.commonMistake: Learners often write “You listen to the teacher.” An imperative already speaks straight to the listener, so the subject is not needed. Begin with the verb: “Listen to the teacher.”
grammar.memoryTip: Picture a coach calling to the team: “Run! Pass! Shoot!” A coach never says “You run”, only the action word. Imperatives are quick, friendly reminders.
grammar.practice: Complete each command with the imperative verb in brackets. | ______ your hands before eating. (wash) | ______ your voice when the teacher is talking. (lower) | ______ to your parents. (listen) | ______ your toys away after playing. (put) | ______ to be on time. (try) | Answer key: 1. Wash, 2. Lower, 3. Listen, 4. Put, 5. Try.

grammar.title: Should and mustn't: advice and rules
grammar.explanation: Modal verbs let us talk about advice and rules. Should offers friendly advice, a good idea. Mustn't states a strong rule, something we are not allowed to do. Both help a community live well together.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
should + base verb (advice): “You should thank the helpers.”
mustn't + base verb (not allowed): “You mustn't ignore a tenant's needs.”
should can open a question: “Should I help you?”
The opposite of should is shouldn't: “You shouldn't be rude.”
grammar.commonMistake: A common slip is “You shouldn't to go.” After a modal verb we use the base verb with no to: “You shouldn't go.” Remember too that must means you have to, while mustn't means you must not.
grammar.memoryTip: Hear should as a friendly guide saying, “This is a good idea!” Hear mustn't as a bright red sign saying, “Stop! Not allowed!”
grammar.practice: Complete each sentence with should or mustn't. | You ______ forget to brush your teeth before bed. | We ______ help our friends when they need it. | You ______ play video games all night. | Pupils ______ listen to the teacher in class. | Answer key: 1. mustn't, 2. should, 3. mustn't, 4. should.

grammar.title: Prepositions of place and direction
grammar.explanation: Prepositions are small words that show where something is, or which way it moves. They make a sentence clear: “The refugee walked towards the building” gives the direction, while “The book is on the shelf” gives the place.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
Direction words, for where something is going: towards, across.
Place words, for where something is: on, in, near, by.
Direction example: “She walked across the street.”
Place examples: “The school is near the library.” / “The toys are in the box.”
grammar.commonMistake: Writers sometimes say “The apples are on the basket.” The apples sit inside it, so the right word is in: “The apples are in the basket.” Ask whether the thing is inside, resting on top, or beside.
grammar.memoryTip: Draw a small map in your mind: in sits inside a box, on rests on a table, near stands close beside, towards points at a sign, across crosses a bridge, and by waits shoulder to shoulder.
grammar.practice: Choose from the box to complete each sentence: across, towards, on, in, near, by. | The bird flew ______ the tall tree. | The kittens are sleeping ______ the basket. | She walked ______ the street to reach the shop. | The pencil is ______ the table. | The library is ______ my school. | Amal stood ______ the road to watch the parade. | Answer key: 1. towards, 2. in, 3. across, 4. on, 5. near, 6. by.

grammar.title: Past Simple and Past Continuous: telling what happened
grammar.explanation: The Past Simple reports actions that already finished: “The lawyer helped many families.” The Past Continuous shows an action still unfolding at a moment in the past: “The merchant was working when the rain started.” Together they let you tell a whole story.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
Past Simple, regular verbs: add -ed: “play” → “played”, “start” → “started”.
Verbs ending in -e take only -d: “like” → “liked”.
Irregular verbs change shape: “go” → “went”, “see” → “saw”, “have” → “had”.
The Past Simple form stays the same for every subject: “I played”, “she played”, “they played”.
Past Continuous: was / were + verb + -ing.
Use was with I, he, she, it: “I was reading.” Use were with you, we, they: “They were playing.”
Join the two tenses with when or while: “She was studying when her friend called.”
grammar.commonMistake: Two slips are common here. “He help many people” needs the finished form: “He helped many people.” And “They were play in the yard” has lost its -ing: “They were playing in the yard.” State verbs such as know and love stay simple, so we write “I knew”, never “I was knowing”.
grammar.memoryTip: The Past Simple is a photograph of a finished moment; the Past Continuous is a film that is still running. Say “I was watching…” and picture the action moving until something interrupts it.
grammar.practice: Part A: write the Past Simple form of the verb in brackets. | Last summer, I ______ (visit) my grandparents. | The teacher ______ (give) us a test last week. | They ______ (play) video games all evening. | She ______ (make) a delicious cake for the party. | He ______ (write) a letter to his friend. | Part B: write the Past Continuous form of the verbs in brackets. | The cat ______ (sleep) on the couch when the doorbell rang. | We ______ (play) outside when it started to rain. | She ______ (read) a book while he ______ (watch) television. | Answer key, Part A: 1. visited, 2. gave, 3. played, 4. made, 5. wrote. Part B: 1. was sleeping, 2. were playing, 3. was reading / was watching.

grammar.title: Strong verbs, similes and question words
grammar.explanation: A strong verb paints a sharper picture of an action, and a simile compares two things using like or as. Question words open the door to information, which is why a reporter reaches for them in every interview.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
Swap a plain verb for a strong one: “run” → “dash” or “sprint”.
Think of something to compare the action to, then join it with like or as: “He dashed like a cheetah.”
Put the simile inside a full sentence: “The caretaker worked like a machine.”
Question words: Who = people, What = things or ideas, Where = places, When = time, Why = reasons, How = the way something is done.
Structure: question word + helping verb + subject + main verb: “What do you like to eat?”
Who can also be the subject on its own: “Who is coming?”
grammar.commonMistake: “He is like a hero” describes who he is, not what he does, so the simile falls flat: write “He fights like a hero.” With questions, the missing helping verb is the usual slip: “What you like?” should be “What do you like?”
grammar.memoryTip: For similes, ask yourself “What is this action like?” before you write. For questions, treat the six question words as detectives, each one hunting a different clue.
grammar.practice: Part A: finish each sentence with your own strong verb and simile. | The cat jumped ______ a ______. | She wrote her story ______ a ______. | The thunder rumbled ______ a ______. | Part B: fill each blank with the correct question word. | ______ is your best friend? | ______ do you go to the park? | ______ do you want for your birthday? | ______ does your family live? | ______ do you like ice cream? | Simile answer key, examples only: 1. like a kangaroo, 2. like a reporter, 3. like a train; your own comparisons may differ. Question-word answer key: 1. Who, 2. When, 3. What, 4. Where, 5. Why.

speaking.title: Speaking 1: Describe a Job
speaking.instructionsAndModelLines:
Choose one job from your Vocabulary list. Get ready to say three sentences about it, using the Present Simple:
“A ______ is a person who ______.”
“A ______ works ______ (where).”
“A ______ helps our community by ______.”
Record yourself. Check: Did you add the s for “he/she” (“A lawyer helps”)? Did you speak clearly?
speaking.aiTutorPrompt: With an adult listening, ask the tutor to check whether I added the -s for he and she, then ask for one better word.

speaking.title: Speaking 2: The Interview Game
speaking.instructionsAndModelLines:
Play with your AI tutor or a partner. One person chooses a job in secret. The other asks questions to guess it:
“What do you do?” → “I build things from wood.”
“Where do you work?” → “I work in a workshop.”
“What do you use?” → “I use a hammer and saw.”
Guess the job! (A carpenter.) Then swap turns.
speaking.aiTutorPrompt: Ask an adult to sit with me while the tutor hides a job and answers my questions, then tell me which question worked best.

speaking.title: Speaking 3: Giving Advice
speaking.instructionsAndModelLines:
Practise giving kind advice about how to treat people in society, using should and mustn't:
“You should thank the people who help you.”
“You should welcome a new immigrant to your school.”
“You mustn't ignore someone who needs help.”
speaking.aiTutorPrompt: With an adult present, ask the tutor to judge whether each piece of advice uses should or mustn't correctly and kindly.

speaking.title: Speaking 4: Word Expert Minute
speaking.origin: Ehel English Content Template v1.2 curriculum expansion
speaking.reviewStatus: Needs re-review (content updated for self-sufficiency pass)
speaking.instructionsAndModelLines:
Choose six words from your Word Wall, such as senator, merchant and tenant.
Speak for one minute. For each word, say the word, give its meaning, and use it in a sentence about your own town.
Ask an adult to time you and to tick every word you explained clearly if one is available, or time yourself with a clock and check your own list afterwards.
speaking.aiTutorPrompt: Ask an adult to time me while the tutor listens to my six word explanations and names the two that were clearest.

speaking.title: Speaking 5: Welcome a New Neighbour
speaking.origin: Ehel English Content Template v1.2 curriculum expansion
speaking.reviewStatus: Needs re-review (content updated for self-sufficiency pass)
speaking.instructionsAndModelLines:
Work with an adult, a partner, or the AI tutor if you are alone. One of you is new to the town, like Omar in Reading 2.
The other gives three pieces of advice with should and one rule with mustn't.
Add a reason to each piece of advice using because, then swap parts and record the second turn.
speaking.aiTutorPrompt: With an adult beside me, ask the tutor to take the part of a new neighbour so I can practise welcoming advice with because.

speaking.title: Speaking 6: Three-Minute Talk About a Local Hero
speaking.origin: Ehel English Content Template v1.2 curriculum expansion
speaking.instructionsAndModelLines:
Plan and record a three-minute talk about a helper you admire in your own town.
Open by naming the helper and the job, give three reasons why the work matters, and close by saying thank you.
Use at least four unit words and one simile, then listen back and mark one thing to improve.
speaking.aiTutorPrompt: Ask an adult to listen to my recording, then ask the tutor for one way to make my opening and my closing stronger.

writing.title: Writing 1: A Role Reflection Paragraph
writing.promptAndInstructions: Choose one job, for example a caretaker, a lawyer, or an engineer. Write four or five sentences about it in the Present Simple. Say who the person is, what they do, where they work, and why their job matters.
writing.modelText: Our school caretaker arrives before anyone else. He sweeps the corridors and empties every bin. He works in the classrooms, the hall and the yard. His job matters because we cannot learn in a dirty room.
writing.sentenceStarter: The job I have chosen is
writing.expectedLength: One organised paragraph of four to five sentences
writing.successCriteria: I named the job; I used the Present Simple with the -s ending; I said where the person works; I gave one reason why the job matters
writing.support: Answer the four questions one at a time, then join the answers into a paragraph.
writing.extension: Add one sentence saying what would go wrong in your town if nobody did this job.

writing.title: Writing 2: A Short Newspaper Article
writing.promptAndInstructions: Write a short article of about six sentences about a local hero or community helper, for example a refugee who started a business, or a carpenter who helped rebuild a school. Give your article a headline in capital letters, like the messenger in the story: “LOCAL HERO HELPS THE TOWN.”
writing.modelText: CARPENTER REBUILDS THE SCHOOL GATE. Karim finished the new gate on Friday morning. He worked for three days with two helpers. Pupils clapped when the gate swung open. Teacher Yasmin said the school felt safer already. Karim answered that every helper simply does what the town needs.
writing.sentenceStarter: My headline in capital letters is
writing.successCriteria: I wrote a headline in capital letters; I told the reader who, what and where; I used at least three unit words; I ended with a quotation or a closing line
writing.support: Plan the headline last, once you know what the most surprising fact is.
writing.extension: Add a short quotation from the helper and punctuate it with speech marks.

writing.title: Writing 3: An Advice Poster
writing.promptAndInstructions: Make a welcome or safety poster for new immigrants or tenants. Write three pieces of advice using should, and one rule using mustn't. For example: “You should say hello to your neighbours.” and “You mustn't be afraid to ask for help.” Then draw a picture to go with it.
writing.modelText: WELCOME TO OUR STREET. You should say hello to your neighbours. You should keep the shared stairs clear. You should ask a tenant if you cannot find the market. You mustn't leave the front door open at night.
writing.expectedLength: One poster title, three advice lines and one rule
writing.successCriteria: I wrote three should lines; I wrote one mustn't rule; I used the base verb after every modal; my poster title is clear from far away
writing.support: Write the four lines first, then choose the largest word for the title.
writing.extension: Turn one should line into a question, such as “Should I knock first?”, and answer it.

writing.title: Writing 4: A Parade Recount
writing.origin: Ehel English Content Template v1.2 curriculum expansion
writing.promptAndInstructions: Retell one part of the parade in six sentences. Begin with a Past Continuous sentence that sets the scene, then use the Past Simple for the events that followed. Use when or while at least once.
writing.modelText: The crowd was waiting quietly when the drums began. The mayor walked first, with the governor behind, and the people clapped. While the dancers turned, an artist painted a bright canvas. A photographer knelt down and took her picture. The messenger rang his bell and shouted the headline. We walked home slowly and talked about every helper.
writing.sentenceStarter: We were waiting by the road when
writing.successCriteria: I opened in the Past Continuous; I used Past Simple verbs for the events; I used when or while once; I kept the events in order
writing.support: List the events in order first, then decide which one was still happening at the start.
writing.extension: Add one sentence with a strong verb and a simile, such as “The drums rolled like thunder.”

writing.title: Writing 5: Refugee and Immigrant Fact File
writing.origin: Ehel English Content Template v1.2 curriculum expansion
writing.promptAndInstructions: Write a fact file with a heading and five accurate sentences that explain the difference between a refugee and an immigrant. Use both words at least twice and finish with one sentence about welcoming people.
writing.modelText: WHO MOVES, AND WHY. A refugee leaves home because it is not safe. An immigrant moves to build a new life. Both may travel a long way. Both need a home, a school and a friend. We should welcome a refugee and an immigrant in the same warm way.
writing.sentenceStarter: My heading for this fact file is
writing.expectedLength: One heading plus five factual sentences
writing.successCriteria: I used refugee twice; I used immigrant twice; every sentence states a fact; my last sentence explains why we welcome both
writing.support: Reread Reading 2 and underline the two sentences that give the contrast.
writing.extension: Add one fact about what a school can do in a newcomer's first week.

writing.title: Writing 6: Revise and Improve Your Article
writing.origin: Ehel English Content Template v1.2 curriculum expansion
writing.promptAndInstructions: Return to your newspaper article. Rewrite three sentences to make them stronger, add two useful details, and write one sentence explaining the best change you made.
writing.modelText: I changed “He worked hard” to “He sanded the gate until it shone.” I added the day and the number of helpers. The best change was the strong verb, because a reader can now picture the work.
writing.sentenceStarter: The sentence I improved most is
writing.expectedLength: Three revised sentences, two added details and one comment
writing.successCriteria: I rewrote three sentences; I added two details; I explained one improvement; I checked capital letters and full stops
writing.support: Read your article aloud and mark the sentence that sounds flattest.
writing.extension: Swap articles with a partner and suggest one improvement to each other.

teacherNotes.note: Model each job word aloud with a gesture before learners read it, and check meaning with a quick thumbs signal before independent work. Device safety: an adult stays present for every AI tutor task in this unit, and no learner works with the tutor alone. Handle the refugee and immigrant passages gently, because some learners may have made such a journey themselves; keep the focus on welcome, never on questioning anybody's story.

Use the AI tutor for three jobs in this unit: rehearsing the interview in Reading 3, checking the -s ending in Present Simple sentences, and giving feedback on the advice poster. Ask learners to read their own sentence aloud first, then have the tutor respond, so the child leads and the tutor confirms. Every vocabulary entry carries its own tutor prompt; keep to those prompts rather than free chat, and stop the session if a learner starts sharing personal details.
